```{python}
#| echo: false
from pbc.authoring import excerpt, lesson_header, reproduce_this, source_link
from pbc.mechanics import kinematics

result = experiment.run()
lesson_header()
```

Open with the question, in the reader's terms and without a heading: what is
puzzling, what goes wrong, what we want to know. No equation, no method, and
no code yet. For the example of this template it could read: a cart is
rolling and the brake goes on. Where does it stop? And if a program moves the
cart forward one small step at a time, does it stop the cart in the same
place?

Then one short paragraph on what the lesson gives the reader to answer the
question, and why the answer can be trusted: here, a motion we can write down
exactly, so that any gap between it and the program belongs to the program.
Do not list what the lesson derives, shows, and measures; that paragraph
would fit any lesson. If the page shows something other than a plain
computation (a measurement, a recorded run of a model, a hypothetical design),
say which here. "What you'll learn" is added by the header above, from
`outcomes`.

## Assumptions

State every assumption of the model and of the program, and for each one what
goes wrong when it does not hold. Keep each short: the complete list lives
here, and the explanation recalls an assumption at the step that uses it. A
capstone puts its design brief first in this section, in words: the
requirements, the constraints, and the success criteria, apart from the
choices the design makes.

1. **First assumption.** What it means, and what breaks without it.
2. **Second assumption.** What it means, and what breaks without it.

## Explanation

Give the reader something to hold before each equation: the situation, the
picture, the one idea the equation will write down. Freeze the cart at one
instant. To say where it will be a moment later you need to know where it is
and how fast it is moving, and the brake says how the speed changes. Equations
are LaTeX and become MathML; two that belong together go in a pair:

::: {.equation-pair}
$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t} = v,
$$

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t} = a(t).
$$
:::

After the equation, say in a sentence what it says: the position changes at
the rate of the velocity, and the velocity at the rate the brake sets. To give
the section a title of its own, keep the identifier:
`## From rates of change to an update rule {#explanation}`.

Say where a derivation is going before the algebra, give each step its reason
in words, and state the result in words afterwards. The derivations the
lesson's question rests on stay here, step by step: the core explanation never
lives behind a link. Only a derivation that is truly optional moves to a
section of its own after the worked examples, linked from here. Label a
statement a reader could take for a result with its claim type
(`observational`, `experimentally-supported`, `numerically-verified`, or
`formal-theorem`; the guide defines each). `scope` and `evidence` are optional.

[The computed position is ahead of the exact one at every time step after the start, and the gap grows with time.]{.claim type="numerically-verified" scope="constant braking, the steps shown" evidence="fig-replace-with-a-name"}

An optional "Go deeper" block names a key of `site/references.yaml`, never a
raw URL. The text is the reason to visit. Delete the block when no source adds
something this lesson does not contain (the guide gives the selection
protocol).

::: {.go-deeper ref="REPLACE-WITH-A-REGISTER-KEY"}
What the source adds that this lesson does not contain, and that the lesson
does not need it.
:::

## Code

Reusable code lives in `src/pbc` with unit tests. Show it by reference; the
listing is read from the file when the site is built. Show a block only when
you can say why the reader meets it at this point. The step below is here
because it is the update rule of the explanation, written as a program: each
term of the equations can be found in it. It is short and its order of
operations is the point, so it is shown whole, as exact source.

```{python}
#| echo: false
excerpt(kinematics.euler_step)
```

A page keeps three kinds of code apart, and the build labels each. Exact
source is the object as the file has it, as above. An exact selection is some
of its lines, unchanged, with a mark where lines are left out; the first
worked example shows one. A derived form is not the source text: the
generated signature, `excerpt(f, signature=True)`, is the only one. Show the
calculations, assumptions, guards, and transformations the conclusions rest
on, and link code that only draws or formats. The guide has the forms and the
rules ("Code").

## Worked examples

### Name of the first example

Start an example from a question and a prediction, not from what the cell
does. The brake takes the same speed off the cart every second, so the exact
motion can be written down. The program moves the cart through each step with
the speed it had when the step began. Before you look at the result: will the
computed cart end ahead of the exact one, or behind it?

Everything the page computes is in the lesson's experiment, which the
header cell runs once as `result`. A cell shows the experiment's code by
reference and its result: a listing, then what it printed or a table. The
first listing is an exact selection, the lines of one named region; choose a
selection so that it reads on its own and ends on a whole statement.

```{python}
#| echo: false
excerpt(experiment, region="setup")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
excerpt(experiment.braking_cart)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
print(result.output("braking-cart"), end="")
```

Put computed numbers into a sentence with an inline expression that reads
the experiment: the exact position is `{python} result["exact-position"]` m. Never type a result by hand;
the check reports a number in the prose that no expression produced. A value
you give, not compute, is marked: the start speed is [2 m/s]{.given}. A table
of results is built with `table()`, not printed; see the guide.

A cell that draws a figure has a `fig-` label, a caption that says what the
figure shows and what to conclude, alternative text that describes its shape,
and a status: `measured`, `calibrated`, `processed`, `simulated`, or
`conceptual`. The function that draws this figure only draws, so its code is
not listed: the Figure source link under the figure opens it. Read a drawing
function before you link it. If it computes something the conclusion rests on
(a residual, an offset, a fit), show those lines as an exact selection.

```{python}
#| label: fig-replace-with-a-name
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Caption shown under the figure."
#| fig-alt: "What a reader who cannot see the figure needs to know: the kind of plot, the axes, and what the curves do."
#| fig-status: simulated
result.show("fig-replace-with-a-name")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
source_link(experiment.draw_replace_with_a_name, figure=True)
```

After each figure or table, say what it means for the question of the lesson,
with where the data came from and what it was checked against. Reporting the
content is not interpreting it. Here: the computed cart is ahead of the exact
one, and the gap grows with every step, because each step moves the cart with
the speed it had when the step began, and the brake lowers that speed while
the step lasts. Both curves are computed; none of this is measured.

A transition says why the next part follows, once: we know the direction of
the error, but not yet its size, and the exercise measures it.

Material that the build does not run or check carries the "not verified"
marker, as a block or inside a sentence:

::: {.not-verified}
```python
state = step(state)  # a sketch that is not executed
```
:::

A measured or quoted value is marked the same way:
[about 9.8 m/s² at sea level]{.not-verified}.

End the worked examples on the conclusion, as the last paragraph before the
limits: what the reader can now do or understand, tied back to the opening
question, and what remains open. We asked whether a program that moves the
cart in small steps stops it where the exact motion does. It does not, and we
can say in which direction it misses and why. What we cannot say yet is how
the miss depends on the size of the step; that is the next lesson's question.

## Limits {#limits}

What the result does not show: where the model or the method fails, and what
was not measured or proved. One paragraph or a short list. A limit is stated
here in full and once; elsewhere it is at most a clause with its scope.
